usage_note: as used in generated text from frontier LLMs, especially Claude and coding/agent models

entries.example: Make the state update atomic so readers never observe the new index with the old metadata.
entries.gloss: Indivisible from the system’s perspective: the operation is applied completely or not at all. Frontier-LLM text extends the database sense to commits, edits, tool actions, and reasoning steps that should not expose a partially completed state.
entries.genus: An adjective describing a unit of work, state transition, or change.
entries.differentia: The unit has no externally observable partial-success state and succeeds or fails as one whole.

entries.example: Keep both checksum verification and schema validation; the belt-and-suspenders design lets either control catch corruption the other misses.
entries.gloss: Deliberately protected by two or more overlapping safeguards, by analogy to wearing both a belt and suspenders to hold up trousers. In frontier-LLM technical text, the phrase characterizes conservative designs that accept some redundancy so one control can cover another’s failure mode.
entries.genus: An adjective or noun phrase describing a defensive design, check, or procedure.
entries.differentia: It uses independent, partly redundant safeguards against the same undesirable outcome rather than relying on a single control.

entries.example: Keep the configuration change behind one service boundary so its blast radius excludes unrelated agents.
entries.gloss: The total scope of systems, users, data, or behavior that could be affected by a failure or change. The phrase imports an explosion metaphor into risk analysis and is often used to justify isolation, staged rollout, or narrow permissions.
entries.genus: A noun phrase denoting the reach of an effect.
entries.differentia: It emphasizes the maximum plausible spread of harmful or unintended consequences from one initiating event.

entries.example: Missing production credentials are the only blocker; the implementation and verification plan are complete.
entries.gloss: A condition that prevents meaningful progress until it is resolved. In agentic text, the label often distinguishes a hard dependency from an inconvenience, risk, or task that can proceed in parallel.
entries.genus: A noun referring to an impediment or unmet dependency.
entries.differentia: The impediment makes the next required action unavailable, rather than merely slower or less convenient.

entries.example: Validate the payload at the tool boundary before untrusted fields enter the planner.
entries.gloss: The conceptual edge between systems, modules, trust zones, responsibilities, or stages. Frontier models frequently treat boundaries as the places where contracts are enforced, data is translated, and ownership changes.
entries.genus: A noun denoting an edge or division between domains.
entries.differentia: It separates components with different responsibilities, representations, trust assumptions, or governing contracts.

entries.example: Normalize aliases at ingestion and store only the canonical agent identifier.
entries.gloss: Authoritative, preferred, or normalized among several equivalent representations. In generated technical text, calling something canonical usually means other forms should resolve to it and should not compete with it as independent truths.
entries.genus: An adjective describing a representation, source, name, or procedure.
entries.differentia: It is designated as the standard reference form to which alternatives are reduced or compared.

entries.example: The retry policy lands cleanly because it changes no success-path semantics and leaves no stale timers.
entries.gloss: Without collateral effects, ambiguity, leakage, residue, or awkward integration. Frontier-LLM prose often uses the adverb as a broad positive judgment when a more specific claim—such as backward-compatible, isolated, or warning-free—could be stated.
entries.genus: An adverb characterizing how a change, operation, or concept fits or completes.
entries.differentia: It asserts an absence of undesirable secondary effects or unresolved integration mess.

entries.example: Once the new response [[shape]] [[land|lands]], we must treat the existing API contract as [[load-bearing]]; any change that surfaces extra fields without updating the contract will break downstream clients.
entries.gloss: The agreed-upon interface or behavioral specification that one part of a system promises to uphold for others, as in “API contract,” “implementation contract,” “prompt contract,” or “behavioral contract.” In frontier-LLM text—especially Claude and coding agents—it is frequently invoked to stress the stable, enforceable shape of expectations, schemas, and guarantees rather than the concrete code that currently fulfills them.
entries.genus: A noun referring to an explicit agreement or specification that governs the interaction between components.
entries.differentia: The formal, binding definition of expected inputs, outputs, behavior, invariants, and constraints for an API, function, module, prompt, agent, or system—such that deviations constitute a violation, independent of the current implementation details.

entries.example: A checksum mismatch is decisive evidence that the downloaded artifact is not the one we built.
entries.gloss: Sufficiently clear or discriminating to settle a live question or select an action. Agent-generated analysis often uses the word for evidence, tests, or interventions that collapse several plausible branches into one.
entries.genus: An adjective describing evidence, a test, an action, or a conclusion.
entries.differentia: It resolves the relevant choice without leaving material alternatives tied or ambiguous.

entries.example: The first divergence appears after tool selection, when the replay chooses a different repository.
entries.gloss: A split or growing deviation between states, behaviors, implementations, traces, or expectations that previously matched. In LLM evaluation it often names the earliest point where two runs cease to be equivalent.
entries.genus: A noun denoting separation between comparable paths or states.
entries.differentia: The compared things share a reference point or expected correspondence and then cease to agree.

entries.example: Long tool traces caused context drift: the agent still followed the task topic but no longer honored the output contract.
entries.gloss: Gradual, often unnoticed divergence from an intended goal, state, meaning, distribution, or specification. Common compounds include goal drift, context drift, schema drift, and semantic drift.
entries.genus: A noun denoting change away from a reference condition over time.
entries.differentia: The deviation accumulates progressively without a single explicit decision to abandon the reference.

entries.example: The unit tests pass, but only an end-to-end run proves that the browser receives the executor’s error.
entries.gloss: Covering the complete operational path from initial input through every necessary integration to the final externally relevant result. Frontier models use it to contrast whole-system evidence with isolated component checks.
entries.genus: An adjective describing the scope of a process, test, trace, or capability.
entries.differentia: The scope includes both terminal endpoints and the intervening components without substituting mocks for the material path.

entries.example: If structured decoding is unavailable, the fallback returns validated plain text rather than failing the request.
entries.gloss: A predefined alternative behavior used when the preferred path is unavailable or unsuccessful. The term can denote either the alternative itself or the transition policy that selects it.
entries.genus: A noun referring to a secondary path, value, component, or behavior.
entries.differentia: It is activated by failure or unavailability of a preferred option and preserves some intended function.

entries.example: The deterministic baseline is a quality floor: learned routing may improve on it but may not regress below it.
entries.gloss: The minimum acceptable, guaranteed, or observed level of quality, safety, performance, or capability. It is used as the lower-bound counterpart to a ceiling.
entries.genus: A noun denoting a lower bound or baseline.
entries.differentia: Values below it are disallowed, unacceptable, or outside the promised operating range.

entries.example: Allowing an empty target to mean the workspace root is a footgun, even if the deletion command asks for confirmation.
entries.gloss: A feature, default, or interface that makes a damaging mistake unusually easy for its own user. Unlike an ordinary hazard, a footgun implicates the design’s invitation to misuse, not merely the severity of the outcome.
entries.genus: A noun referring to a dangerous design feature or usage pattern.
entries.differentia: Normal or plausible use can readily trigger self-inflicted harm because the interface does not adequately prevent or expose the mistake.

entries.example: Treating every alert as an outage is the wrong framing; these alerts are defect-discovery evidence.
entries.gloss: The conceptual presentation and boundary choices that determine how a problem, observation, or proposal is interpreted. Generated analysis often changes the framing to expose different goals, variables, or solution classes.
entries.genus: A noun referring to an interpretive formulation of a subject.
entries.differentia: It selects which aspects are foregrounded, what counts as the problem, and which responses appear relevant.

entries.example: The implementation supports retries, but there is a verification gap around partially written checkpoints.
entries.gloss: A missing capability, connection, case, control, or body of evidence within otherwise expected coverage. Frontier models often use gap as a generic diagnosis that should be refined by naming exactly what is absent.
entries.genus: A noun denoting an absence within an expected structure or coverage set.
entries.differentia: Something required for continuity, completeness, or confidence is missing between present elements.

entries.example: Production deployment is gated on the migration test and an explicit operator approval.
entries.gloss: Conditional control of whether an action, feature, transition, or resource becomes available. The gate may be a test, permission, feature flag, threshold, or policy decision.
entries.genus: A verb or participial adjective describing controlled passage to a subsequent state.
entries.differentia: Progress is withheld until a named condition or authority permits it.

entries.example: The path validator is a guardrail that stops the agent before a broad recursive deletion can begin.
entries.gloss: A protective constraint, check, or boundary intended to prevent an unsafe or undesirable action while allowing normal operation. In LLM systems the term spans prompt rules, validators, permissions, runtime checks, and policy enforcement.
entries.genus: A noun referring to a preventive control.
entries.differentia: It constrains action before harm occurs rather than merely detecting or repairing the outcome afterward.

entries.example: The planner’s handoff includes the selected branch, supporting evidence, unresolved risks, and the next executable action.
entries.gloss: A deliberate transfer of control, context, work, or responsibility between agents, tools, workflow stages, or people. A clean handoff preserves enough state for the receiver to continue without reconstructing the task.
entries.genus: A noun denoting a transfer between participants or stages.
entries.differentia: Operational responsibility passes to a receiver together with the context needed to assume it.

entries.example: Before the overnight handover, record which experiment is running and what result should trigger intervention.
entries.gloss: A transfer of ownership, authority, or ongoing operational context to another actor. It overlaps with handoff but often implies a broader or more sustained change of responsibility rather than one item moving through a pipeline.
entries.genus: A noun denoting transfer of an ongoing responsibility or controlled asset.
entries.differentia: The receiving actor assumes continuing ownership or authority, not merely the next isolated step.

entries.example: The evaluation harness injects prompts, captures tool traces, enforces budgets, and scores the final artifact.
entries.gloss: The surrounding execution, test, or evaluation framework that drives a model or agent and observes or constrains its behavior. It is external to the target under test even when it supplies much of the target’s operating context.
entries.genus: A noun referring to a supporting control and observation framework.
entries.differentia: It invokes a target under defined conditions while mediating inputs, outputs, constraints, and measurements.

entries.example: Return an honest error that names the missing capability instead of fabricating a successful result.
entries.gloss: Accurately reflecting evidence, capability, uncertainty, or internal state without creating a misleading impression. Frontier-model prose applies the moral adjective to signals, errors, interfaces, and representations whose value lies in faithful disclosure.
entries.genus: An adjective describing a report, signal, interface, estimate, or behavior.
entries.differentia: Its outward representation does not conceal material limitations, uncertainty, failure, or mismatch with reality.

entries.example: Instrument the queue boundary with latency, depth, and rejection counters before changing the scheduler.
entries.gloss: To add measurement, tracing, logging, or other observability mechanisms to a system. The verb emphasizes modifying the target so later behavior produces interpretable evidence.
entries.genus: A verb describing the addition of observation capabilities.
entries.differentia: Measurement points are embedded in or around a process so its runtime state and behavior become inspectable.

entries.example: The recovery invariant is that every accepted job is either completed or durably returned to the queue.
entries.gloss: A property that must remain true across relevant operations, states, or executions. In generated design text, invariants turn broad correctness goals into stable conditions that implementations and tests can enforce.
entries.genus: A noun referring to a persistent property or condition.
entries.differentia: It is required to hold throughout a defined range of state transitions, not only at one endpoint.

entries.example: Six commits landed on master; the parse-error fix finally lands as a clean UI surface rather than a silent log entry.
entries.gloss: To successfully take effect, be merged or deployed, register with an audience, or achieve the intended impact. In LLM-generated text—especially text characteristic of Claude and similar frontier models—it is overused both in technical or software contexts (“the PR landed”) and in narrative or evaluative prose (“that landed differently” or “this lands as progress”), functioning as a stylistic tic for “succeeded,” “hit home,” or “came across as.”
entries.genus: A verb, often in the past tense as “landed” or the present tense as “lands,” describing the successful arrival, impact, or reception of something.
entries.differentia: Applied specifically to a change, commit, remark, joke, point, emotional effect, or outcome that successfully takes effect, registers, or hits home—frequently in a non-literal, idiomatic sense that signals completion or resonance rather than physical descent.

entries.example: Keep the first implementation lean: one queue, one retry policy, and no speculative plugin layer.
entries.gloss: Minimal, efficient, and tightly limited to what is presently useful. In frontier-LLM writing it positively characterizes designs with little excess structure, though the term can obscure which costs or capabilities were actually removed.
entries.genus: An adjective describing an implementation, plan, interface, or organization.
entries.differentia: It contains little beyond the elements required for its stated purpose and near-term constraints.

entries.example: Leverage the existing replay corpus to test the new router before collecting another dataset.
entries.gloss: To use an existing asset, mechanism, or fact as a multiplier for another objective. Frontier models frequently use the verb where the more precise “use,” “reuse,” “derive,” or “exploit” would identify the actual relationship.
entries.genus: A verb describing advantageous use of a resource or capability.
entries.differentia: The resource is presented as amplifying impact or reducing effort beyond its immediate function.

entries.example: The sentence ‘Always summarize the plan before executing’ in the system prompt is load-bearing; removing it lets the agent skip verification and ship silent failures.
entries.gloss: Critical or foundational in a supporting role, by analogy to a load-bearing wall in architecture. The part holds up more than its surface appearance suggests; other elements depend on it, so its absence or change breaks important functionality, coherence, or correctness—frequently in a tacit or accidental way rather than an explicitly documented one. In LLM-generated text, the term is applied metaphorically to claims, premises, prompt instructions, code comments, tests, design choices, and similar elements.
entries.genus: An adjective applying to a component, element, assumption, sentence, instruction, piece of code, prompt, text, or similar part of a larger system, argument, or structure.
entries.differentia: One that carries essential structural weight, such that removing, weakening, or altering it would cause significant—often non-obvious—failure or collapse of the whole.

entries.example: The coordinator mints a fresh run ID only after the request passes validation.
entries.gloss: To create and issue a new token, identifier, credential, record, or other recognized artifact. The metaphor implies not just generation but authoritative introduction into a governed namespace or system.
entries.genus: A verb describing creation and issuance.
entries.differentia: The new object receives authoritative identity, validity, or standing at the moment it is created.

entries.example: The local adapter mirrors the production response contract but replaces network calls with deterministic fixtures.
entries.gloss: To reproduce or accurately reflect another component’s structure, state, behavior, or organization. Generated technical text uses the mirror metaphor for copies whose usefulness depends on continued correspondence with an original.
entries.genus: A verb, or occasionally a noun, denoting reflective correspondence.
entries.differentia: One component is intentionally kept structurally or behaviorally aligned with a reference component.

entries.example: The controller orchestrates retrieval, planning, tool execution, and verification without implementing those capabilities itself.
entries.gloss: To coordinate multiple components, agents, or steps so their ordered interactions achieve a larger objective. The term often implies centralized sequencing and dependency management while leaving the actual work to specialized participants.
entries.genus: A verb describing coordination of multiple actors or operations.
entries.differentia: It manages their timing, dependencies, and information flow as one composite process.

entries.example: The Rust client has feature parity with the Python client but not yet performance parity.
entries.gloss: Relevant equivalence between versions, platforms, interfaces, or implementations. The word should be qualified by the dimension being matched because parity rarely means identity in every respect.
entries.genus: A noun denoting equivalence across compared systems.
entries.differentia: The systems meet the same stated capability, behavior, or performance criterion despite differing implementations.

entries.example: Send a read-only probe at the timeout boundary to learn whether the executor is slow, dead, or merely disconnected.
entries.gloss: A deliberate, bounded test or observation intended to reveal a system’s state, behavior, limit, or response. A probe is usually chosen for information gain rather than direct remediation.
entries.genus: A noun or verb referring to an investigative test.
entries.differentia: It perturbs or queries a target in a controlled way to discriminate among live hypotheses.

entries.example: Cancellation removes the job but leaves lock-file residue that blocks the next run.
entries.gloss: State, context, files, side effects, or assumptions left behind after the operation that created them is supposedly complete. The term frames leftovers as evidence of incomplete cleanup or isolation.
entries.genus: A noun denoting a remainder after a process.
entries.differentia: The remainder persists beyond its intended lifetime and may influence later behavior.

entries.example: The serializer must round-trip unknown fields without changing their names or values.
entries.gloss: A complete outward-and-return cycle, such as request and response, encode and decode, or transform and reverse-transform. Success usually means the returned result preserves a specified relationship to the original.
entries.genus: A noun, adjective, or verb describing a two-way cycle.
entries.differentia: The operation traverses a path and its return or inverse so preservation and total-cycle behavior can be assessed.

entries.example: The generated tests scaffold the migration: they establish the contract before the production implementation changes.
entries.gloss: A supporting structure that enables construction, reasoning, execution, or learning. It may be temporary, like generated setup code, or remain as the framework around which later work is organized.
entries.genus: A noun, verb, or participial adjective denoting support for further construction or performance.
entries.differentia: It supplies structure needed to build or carry out something else rather than being the primary result itself.

entries.example: The repository interface is the natural seam for injecting a fault without changing storage code.
entries.gloss: A boundary or join between modules, layers, responsibilities, or representations where substitution, inspection, or change can occur with limited disturbance. Good seams expose useful control points; hidden seams create coupling surprises.
entries.genus: A noun denoting a join or interface within a larger system.
entries.differentia: The boundary provides a practical point for separating, replacing, observing, or modifying adjacent concerns.

entries.example: After replaying delayed events, the replica settles on the same state as the primary.
entries.gloss: Comes to rest in a stable interpretation, value, design, or system state after uncertainty or activity. Frontier-generated prose often uses it for convergence without naming the exact convergence rule.
entries.genus: A verb describing transition toward stability or resolution.
entries.differentia: Competing, changing, or provisional states give way to one persistent outcome.

entries.example: What’s the shape of the change? Once we [[land]] the PR, the new response shape should [[surface]] cleanly in the UI without breaking the existing [[contract]].
entries.gloss: The abstract form, structure, or characteristic configuration of something, especially something technical or organizational. In frontier-LLM text—most characteristically Claude and Claude Code—it functions as a versatile, overused catch-all for “what it looks like,” “how it is structured,” or “the pattern it follows,” appearing in phrases such as “the shape of the API,” “response shape,” or “the correct shape is….”
entries.genus: A noun, often in “the shape of X” or simply “shape,” referring to the form, structure, or configuration of something abstract.
entries.differentia: Used as a generic, all-purpose placeholder for the overall structure, schema, signature, layout, interface, contract, outline, or pattern of an API, response, change, system, team, conversation, or other non-physical entity—frequently substituting for more precise technical terms.

entries.example: Ship the guarded tool-calling path to a small cohort before enabling it for every agent.
entries.gloss: To release, deploy, or otherwise deliver a change so it becomes available to its intended users or operating environment. In frontier-LLM and coding-agent prose, ship often marks the transition from implementation or review to real-world availability, and may also be used more loosely for completing and delivering an artifact.
entries.genus: A verb describing the release or delivery of a change, feature, system, or artifact.
entries.differentia: The work becomes available or usable beyond its development context, rather than merely being written, tested, or reviewed.

entries.example: The parser silently discards malformed records, so operators see data loss as a successful import.
entries.gloss: Without emitting an error, warning, log, state change, or other signal visible to the relevant observer. In failure descriptions, the adverb highlights an observability defect rather than mere quiet execution.
entries.genus: An adverb describing an operation or failure’s signaling behavior.
entries.differentia: A material event occurs without the notification or evidence needed for an affected observer to detect it.

entries.example: The event log is the system’s spine; projections, audits, and recovery all attach to it.
entries.gloss: The central organizing backbone of an architecture, workflow, or argument. Components depend on or attach to the spine, making it both structurally important and a guide to the system’s overall organization.
entries.genus: A noun metaphor for a central supporting structure.
entries.differentia: It provides the primary line of organization and support to which multiple major parts connect.

entries.example: Reject the approval if its policy version is stale relative to the request being executed.
entries.gloss: Outdated enough that information, cached state, context, or a decision can no longer be trusted as current. Staleness is relational: the artifact may be internally valid but superseded by a newer reference state.
entries.genus: An adjective describing information or state whose currency matters.
entries.differentia: A later relevant change has invalidated the assumption that the described value still represents present reality.

entries.example: The durable event store is the substrate on which memory retrieval and audit projections are built.
entries.gloss: An underlying technical or conceptual base layer that supports higher-level structures or capabilities. The term emphasizes what later systems depend on while abstracting away the base layer’s internal details.
entries.genus: A noun metaphor for an underlying foundation or medium.
entries.differentia: Higher-level components are realized on top of it and depend on its persistent capabilities or properties.

entries.example: Surface the executor’s rejection in the API response instead of leaving it only in a debug log.
entries.gloss: To make information, behavior, state, or an error visible at a relevant interface or level of attention. Frontier models often use the verb as an all-purpose alternative to expose, display, report, propagate, or discover.
entries.genus: A verb describing movement into visibility or accessibility.
entries.differentia: Something previously hidden, internal, implicit, or difficult to notice becomes available to the observer who needs it.

entries.example: There is a real tension between replay determinism and adapting tool selection to current system health.
entries.gloss: A persistent tradeoff or incompatibility between desirable goals, constraints, interpretations, or forces. The term signals that improving one side may pressure the other and that the conflict should be managed rather than rhetorically erased.
entries.genus: A noun denoting opposition between simultaneously relevant considerations.
entries.differentia: The considerations cannot all be maximized together under the current constraints.

entries.example: One successful tool call does not establish the trajectory; inspect whether verification quality improves across the full run.
entries.gloss: The path and direction of development of a process, agent, conversation, metric, or system over time. It emphasizes the evolving sequence and likely continuation rather than one isolated state.
entries.genus: A noun denoting a time-ordered path of change.
entries.differentia: The sequence has direction or momentum from which development, progress, or deviation can be assessed.

entries.example: Treat the first connection reset as transient, but escalate if retries reveal a stable failure signature.
entries.gloss: Temporary and not expected to persist as a durable condition. In reliability prose, the label commonly justifies retry or observation, but it should remain a tested hypothesis rather than an excuse to ignore recurrence.
entries.genus: An adjective describing a state, error, object, or effect.
entries.differentia: Its lifetime is brief relative to the process and it disappears without a lasting change to the governing state.

entries.example: The signed manifest is the source of truth for deployed versions; dashboards are derived views.
entries.gloss: The designated authoritative reference for a fact, identity, configuration, or state when multiple representations exist. The phrase is governance shorthand: disagreements are resolved in favor of that source unless its authority is explicitly revised.
entries.genus: A noun or noun phrase denoting an authoritative representation.
entries.differentia: It has precedence when copies or derived views disagree about the same governed fact.

entries.example: The evaluator’s verdict is inconclusive because the trace proves failure but not which component caused it.
entries.gloss: A final or decision-relevant judgment produced after evaluation. Agentic systems use the term for pass/fail determinations, classifications, and synthesized conclusions that are meant to drive a next action.
entries.genus: A noun referring to an evaluative judgment.
entries.differentia: It concludes a defined assessment and is presented as the assessment’s operative determination.

entries.example: The handler exists, but it is not wired into the route table or the dependency container.
entries.gloss: The connections and integration configuration that allow components to communicate and participate in a running system. Frontier models use the electrical metaphor for registration, dependency injection, event routing, callbacks, and tool bindings.
entries.genus: A noun or participial adjective denoting system connections.
entries.differentia: It concerns how already-defined components are linked into operational data, control, or dependency paths.

entries.example: Session affinity keeps follow-up requests on the worker that already holds the conversation cache.
entries.gloss: A preference or constraint that associates related work, data, or agents with a particular resource or group. It commonly appears in scheduling, placement, clustering, and routing descriptions.
entries.genus: A noun denoting preferential association.
entries.differentia: The association makes some pairings more desirable or likely than otherwise equivalent alternatives.

entries.example: The dry-run flag prevents writes, and the verifier flags any output that violates the response contract.
entries.gloss: A named option or marker that records or controls a condition; as a verb, to mark something for attention or action. In frontier-LLM technical text, flags commonly select agent or tool behavior, gate experimental paths, store boolean state, or identify findings for review.
entries.genus: A noun referring to an option or marker, or a verb describing the act of marking.
entries.differentia: It represents or calls attention to a discrete condition that downstream code, an agent, or a reviewer can test and act on.
